question: The rate at which consumers convert the chemical energy in their food into their biomass is called:
solution:
The correct answer is __**secondary productivity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Secondary productivity refers to the rate at which consumers (heterotrophs) convert the chemical energy of their food into their own biomass.
 
• This process is crucial for energy transfer within food webs and ecosystems, as it reflects the efficiency of energy conversion from one trophic level to another.
 
• Secondary productivity is influenced by factors such as the quality and quantity of food available, the metabolic rate of the consumers, and environmental conditions.
 
• It is measured in units of energy (such as joules or calories) or biomass (such as grams) per unit area per unit time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Primary Productivity**

 
 
• Primary productivity is the rate at which energy is converted by photosynthetic and chemosynthetic autotrophs to organic substances.
 
• Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) is the total rate of photosynthesis in a given area.
 
• Net Primary Productivity (NPP) is the rate of energy storage as biomass after accounting for the energy lost through respiration.
 
 
 
• **Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)**
 
 
• GPP is the total amount of energy captured by producers in an ecosystem through photosynthesis over a specific time period.
 
• It represents the total primary production before any energy is used for respiration.
 
 
 
• **Net Primary Productivity (NPP)**
 
 
• NPP is the energy that remains after subtracting the energy producers use for respiration from the GPP.
 
• NPP is the energy available to herbivores and other consumers in the ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Tertiary Productivity**
 
 
• Though not a commonly used term, tertiary productivity would refer to the rate at which higher-level consumers (such as predators) convert their food into biomass.
 
• This level of productivity is usually encompassed within secondary productivity, which includes all consumers.
